h: The Blessing of Bilam Can Strengthen Without Excusing Sin

p: "They sought to establish the passage of Balak
אֶלָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר אָבִין
Rather, said Rabbi Yosei bar Avin:
because this verse is written in it (Bamidbar 24:9):
'He crouched, he lay down like a lion,
and like a lioness — who will rouse him?'"
that it resembles "when you lie down and when you rise,"
that HaKadosh Baruch Hu guards us
when we lie down and when we rise.
וְקָשֶׁה מַה זֶּה שַׁיָּיכוּת לִקְרִיאַת שְׁמַע
But it is difficult: what connection does this have to Krias Shema,
which is accepting the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven
and to speak words of Torah
"when you lie down and when you rise"
"Behold, a people that rises like a lioness, etc.,"
and writes that so it is in the Tanchuma;
and indeed in the Midrash Rabbah and Tanchuma
regarding Krias Shema of morning and evening;
regarding their wish to establish it in Krias Shema.
And Rashi, of blessed memory, too
עַל פָּסוּק הֶן עָם כְּלָבִיא וְגוֹ׳
on the pasuk "Behold, a people like a lioness, etc.,"
he did not emend to this pasuk.
אַךְ אִיתָא בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רַבָּה (רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת דְּבָרִים)
But it is brought in the Midrash Rabbah (beginning of Devarim):
מוֹכִיחַ אָדָם אַחֲרַי חֵן יִמְצָא (מִשְׁלֵי כח, כג)
"'He who rebukes a man will in the end find more favor' (Mishlei 28:23)
'than one who flatters with the tongue'
And that is in what he said,
כָּל הַקּוֹרֵא קְרִיאַת שְׁמַע עַל מִטָּתוֹ
"Whoever recites Krias Shema upon his bed
כְּאִלּוּ אוֹחֵז חֶרֶב שֶׁל שְׁתֵּי פִיּוֹת בְּיָדוֹ וְכוּלֵּי
is as if he holds a double-edged sword in his hand, etc.,"
"and a double-edged sword in their hand" (Tehillim 149:6).
And although it is written afterward,
"to execute vengeance upon the nations, etc.,"
the main intent of the double-edged sword
is to slay the yetzer hara,
"the harmful spirits keep away from him."
correspond to the two roots of the kelipos:
35 from the right and 35 from the left,
the kelipah of Esav and the kelipah of Yishmael.
And the main fear is at night,
"When you lie down you will not fear";
"And you shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid"
אַךְ שָׁם יֵשׁ לְפָרֵשׁ פַּחַד וַחֲרָדָה
but there one can explain fear and terror
from the coming of an enemy as well.
sixty mighty men are around it, etc.,
because of fear in the nights"
and if it is because of fear of an enemy,
what would sixty mighty men help?
"and for strength to those who turn back the battle":
this is one who overcomes his yetzer;
And this is the meaning of "of the mighty men of Yisrael":
And similar to what it says (Berachos 14a):
כָּל הַמַּשְׂבִּיעַ עַצְמוֹ מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה וְלָן
"Whoever sates himself with words of Torah and goes to sleep
'He shall abide satisfied; he shall not be visited by evil'";
וְהוּא גַּם כֵּן מְרַמֵּז עַל פְּגָם זֶה
and this too alludes to this blemish,
which is called "evil in the eyes of Hashem,"
that there are seventy facets to the Torah,
there are six orders of Mishnah,
corresponding to the six days of the week;
which is the middah of Malchus,
and this is "sixty mighty men, etc."
"'Gird your sword upon your thigh, O mighty one,
this is written about words of Torah."
And this is "all of them hold swords,
"each with his sword upon his thigh,"
כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב חֲגוֹר חַרְבְּךָ עַל יָרֵךְ
as it says, "Gird your sword upon your thigh";
that is, that through words of Torah
he will be saved and guarded from this blemish;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק א רב, א)
as it says in the holy Zohar (Zohar I 202a):
And this is "O mighty one, your glory and your majesty":
for the middah of the Tzaddik who guards the covenant
is called "beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance,"
as it says about Yosef HaTzaddik;
that is, that his body was clean and beautiful,
And as our holy master said,
"Are you not like the children of the Kushim to Me, etc.,"
in Amos refers to this blemish;
for one who blemishes it is called a Kushi and ugly.
And this is "because of fear in the nights."

p: of the Arizal, on this parashah,
he asks why the Torah mentions
"May my soul die the death of the upright,"
for he died by the sword.
that when he said "may my soul die,"
לֹא הָיָה כַּוָּנָתוֹ עַל מִיתַת הַגּוּף
his intent was not the death of the body
but the life of the soul,
which is the World to Come;
וּכְעֵין דְּאִיתָא בַּזּוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (חֵלֶק ג קכז, א)
similar to what is brought in the holy Zohar (Zohar III 127a)
that he has no share in that world.
'Let my soul die with the Pelishtim, etc.'"
That is, from his saying "let my soul die,"
meaning the death of the soul for the World to Come,
שֶׁרָצָה לִמְסוֹר גַּם חֶלְקוֹ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
for he wished to give up even his share in the World to Come
was about the death of the soul for the World to Come,
that he be among the upright.
Now the perception and grasp of Bilam
did not extend to the tzaddikim
כִּי הוּא לֹא הָיָה לוֹ הַשָּׂגָה בָּהֶם
for he had no perception of them;
rather, all his perception and vision
was only of the sinners of Yisrael,
who have no share in the World to Come.
And in the Mishnah at the beginning of Perek Chelek
who have no share in the World to Come:
and one of the four is Bilam.
the beginning of the chapter is,
כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
"All Yisrael have a share in the World to Come,
so what connection does Bilam have
when he is not included among them?
But the matter of the number,
and they are included in the seven middos
opposite the seven middos in holiness.
וְג׳ מְלָכִים הֵם לְעוּמַּת ג׳ הָאָבוֹת
And the three kings are opposite the three Avos,
and corresponding to them in the kelipah
are three kings and four commoners.
the Men of the Great Assembly, who did the counting,
sought to count one more from Yisrael;
for it was difficult for them
to count Bilam among the seven
what is his business among Klal Yisrael?
וּבִקְּשׁוּ לִמְנוֹת שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
And they sought to count Shlomo HaMelech, alav hashalom,
who was a chariot for the middah of Malchus,
and of whom it is written that he blemished so much;
and they wished to count him as the seventh,
which corresponds to the middah of Malchus,
until a bas kol went forth,
and they counted Bilam as the seventh.
And the expounders of allusions would say:
all of them come to the World to Come
And had one been counted, Heaven forbid,
But in truth, in the seventh middah,
there is no blemish at all;
and therefore the expounders of allusions found
that all of them come to the World to Come;
and there remained written in the Mishnah
three kings and three commoners from Yisrael,
and Bilam was counted with them as the seventh.
And this was effected by his prayer,
"May my soul die the death of the upright":
that he was counted among Yisrael
who have no share in the World to Come;
"May my soul die the death of the upright,"
that he be counted with them.

p: וְזֶה עִנְיַן מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב בַּמִּדְרָשׁ (בְּמִדְבַּר פָּרָשָׁה ב)
And this is the matter of what is written in the Midrash (Bamidbar Rabbah 2):
compared them to the stars, etc.;
but Hoshea, who was in the middle,
how can one say of Hoshea
that he did not love Yisrael,
saw only the tzaddikim of Yisrael,
therefore he compared them to the stars,
עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב (מְגִילָּה טז, א)
along the lines of what is written (Megillah 16a):
they rise up to the stars."
therefore he compared them to dust,
they descend down to the dust."
וְזֶהוּ הַפֵּירוּשׁ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ רַבָּה (דְּבָרִים הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל)
And this is the meaning in the Midrash Rabbah (Devarim, mentioned above):
"than one who flatters with the tongue"
That is, in that he gave them confidence
that no Jew will be lost,
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יָכוֹל לִסְמוֹךְ עַל זֶה
and thereby one could rely on this
And although the truth is so,
will not be lost, Heaven forbid,
yet they will suffer beforehand a great deal
until they are refined and purified.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בַּגְּמָרָא (חֲגִיגָה טז, א)
And about this they said in the Gemara (Chagigah 16a):
"'Do not trust in a friend' (Michah 7:5), etc.
if the yetzer hara says to you,
'Sin, and HaKadosh Baruch Hu will forgive,'
And Bilam flattered with his prophecies
that HaKadosh Baruch Hu will refine
"Behold, a people that rises like a lioness
and lifts itself up like a lion";
and in this pasuk the reverse:
"He crouched, he lay down like a lion,
and like a lioness — who will rouse him?"
אַךְ שָׁם מְדַבֵּר לְפִי סֵדֶר הַקִּימָה בַּיּוֹם
But there it speaks according to the order of rising in the day:
at first he strengthens himself only like a lioness,
and afterward "like a lion he lifts himself up."
עַל דֶּרֶךְ מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר (שׁוֹפְטִים ה, כז)
along the lines of what is said (Shoftim 5:27),
that even though he fell, Heaven forbid,
nevertheless "he lay down like a lion":
that he strengthen himself like a lion to return;
וְאַף אִם יִפּוֹל אַחַר כָּךְ מִמַּדְרֵגָתוֹ
and even if he falls afterward from his level
nevertheless he will be like a lioness
and even if he falls once more,
And it follows what is written
אִם עֲוֹנוֹת תִּשְׁמָר יָהּ (תְּהִלִּים קל, ג)
"'If You, Kah, keep account of iniquities' (Tehillim 130:3)
and all levels are closed off in judgment, etc.,
for all the paths of teshuvah
That is, "Mi" equals fifty in gematria,
"and his heart will understand and he will return, etc."
And this is the thought of teshuvah,
And this is what Bilam came to do
with the flattery of his tongue,
that even after all the falls,
and he falls again like a lioness and falls,
And this is what it says,
that through this they fell at Shittim.
And in truth the words are true,
that a person's heart should not fall,
will not be cast away, Heaven forbid,
and he will be refined and whitened
And this is the meaning in the Gemara,
"They sought to establish the passage of Balak
which is accepting the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven
and the yoke of Torah and the yoke of mitzvos.
Lest the heart of a person fall,
one who knows the afflictions of his heart,
the yoke of Torah and the yoke of mitzvos?"
עַל זֶה רָצוּ לִקְבּוֹעַ פָּרָשַׁת בָּלָק
for this they wished to establish the passage of Balak
that it be a source of strength,
as indeed the truth is so,
that "none of them will be cast away,"
and he will be refined in the end,
but that is only for the World to Come.
And on Shabbos, about which it says (Tehillim 92:2),
and it is brought in Pirkei d'Rabbi Eliezer:
"one who confesses and forsakes will be shown mercy"
for Shabbos is a time of teshuvah;
and so it is in the Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah 22):
"Such is the power of teshuvah, etc.;
'A psalm, a song for the day of Shabbos,' etc."
And whoever takes it to heart
and wishes to improve his deeds
can merit a semblance of the World to Come,
